subject: computing
title: KS3 Computing — Network Types & Hardware
subtitle: LAN, WAN, network topologies, hardware components, and wired vs wireless connections.

data.targetWord: Two or more devices connected together so they can share data and resources such as printers, files, and internet access

examples.en-GB: A school network connects hundreds of computers so staff and pupils can share files, printers, and internet access.

data.targetWord: Local Area Network — a network covering a small geographical area such as a single building, school, or office, owned and managed by the organisation using it

examples.en-GB: A school's computer network is a LAN because it covers only the school buildings and is owned by the school.

data.targetWord: Wide Area Network — a network spanning a large geographical area such as a country or the entire globe, using public infrastructure owned by telecommunications companies

examples.en-GB: The Internet is the largest WAN in the world, connecting billions of devices across every country.

data.targetWord: A network device that connects a LAN to the internet or to other networks, routing data packets toward their destination using IP addresses

examples.en-GB: The router at home connects the home LAN to the internet and assigns IP addresses to all connected devices via DHCP.

data.targetWord: A network device that connects multiple devices within a LAN and sends incoming data only to the specific destination device, rather than broadcasting to all devices

examples.en-GB: A switch is more efficient than a hub because it sends each packet only to the device it is addressed to, reducing unnecessary network traffic.

data.targetWord: An older network device that connects devices within a LAN by broadcasting all incoming data to every connected device, regardless of which device it is addressed to

examples.en-GB: Hubs have largely been replaced by switches because broadcasting to all devices wastes bandwidth and creates a security risk.

data.targetWord: Network Interface Card — the hardware component inside a device that enables it to connect to a network; every NIC has a unique MAC address

examples.en-GB: Every computer needs a NIC to join a network; it converts data between the computer's internal format and the signal sent over the network.

data.targetWord: Wireless Access Point — a device connected to a wired network that broadcasts a Wi-Fi signal, allowing wireless devices to join the network

examples.en-GB: The white boxes mounted on classroom walls are WAPs that allow tablets and laptops to connect wirelessly to the school LAN.

data.targetWord: A wired networking technology that uses cables (typically Cat5e or Cat6) to connect devices, offering fast and reliable data transfer

examples.en-GB: Desktop computers in a school computer lab are connected via Ethernet cables for fast, reliable, and secure network access.

data.targetWord: A wireless networking technology that allows devices to connect to a network using radio waves rather than physical cables

examples.en-GB: Wi-Fi lets smartphones and laptops connect to the internet from anywhere within range of a wireless access point.

data.targetWord: A network layout in which every device is connected individually to a central switch; failure of one device does not affect others, but failure of the switch brings down the whole network

examples.en-GB: Most modern schools and offices use star topology because it is reliable and easy to add or remove individual devices.

data.targetWord: A network layout in which all devices connect to a single shared cable called the bus or backbone; a break anywhere in the cable brings down the entire network

examples.en-GB: Bus topology is cheap to install but unreliable — if the backbone cable is damaged, every device on the network loses connection.

data.targetWord: A network layout in which devices are connected in a closed loop, each device connecting to the next; data travels around the ring in one direction

examples.en-GB: Ring topology is less common today; a single break in the ring can disrupt communication for all devices on the network.

data.targetWord: The maximum amount of data that can be transmitted over a network connection in a given time, usually measured in megabits per second (Mbps) or gigabits per second (Gbps)

examples.en-GB: Streaming 4K video requires high bandwidth; if too many users share a connection, each gets a smaller share of the available bandwidth.

data.targetWord: A unique numerical identifier assigned to each device on a network, used by routers to direct data packets to the correct destination

examples.en-GB: Every device connected to the internet has an IP address, such as 192.168.1.5, which acts like a postal address for data.

data.targetWord: Media Access Control address — a unique 48-bit hardware address permanently assigned to every NIC at the time of manufacture, used to identify devices within a LAN

examples.en-GB: A switch uses MAC addresses to send data only to the correct device; no two NICs share the same MAC address.

data.targetWord: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol — a protocol used by routers to automatically assign IP addresses to devices when they join a network

examples.en-GB: When your laptop connects to Wi-Fi, the router uses DHCP to automatically give it an IP address without you having to type one in.

data.targetWord: A small chunk of data that a message is broken into before being sent across a network; each packet contains a header with addressing information and a payload with the actual data

examples.en-GB: When you send an email, it is broken into packets that travel across the network and are reassembled at the destination.

data.targetWord: Any device connected to a network — including computers, printers, switches, routers, and servers — that can send or receive data

examples.en-GB: In a star topology, every computer, printer, and server is a node connected to the central switch.

data.targetWord: A device or program that requests services or data from a server on a network — for example, a computer requesting a web page from a web server

examples.en-GB: Your laptop acts as a client when it requests a web page; it sends the request to a web server and waits for the response.

data.targetWord: A powerful computer on a network that provides services, data, or resources to client devices — for example, a file server stores shared files

examples.en-GB: A school file server stores all pupils' work centrally so it can be accessed from any computer on the network.

data.targetWord: A network security device or software that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic, blocking unauthorised access

examples.en-GB: A school's firewall blocks access to inappropriate websites and prevents unauthorised users from connecting to the school network.

data.targetWord: Internet Service Provider — a company that provides customers with access to the internet, typically via broadband connections

examples.en-GB: BT, Sky, and Virgin Media are ISPs that provide home broadband connections to millions of UK households.

data.targetWord: A high-speed internet connection that provides fast data transfer, allowing multiple users to access the internet simultaneously

examples.en-GB: Fibre optic broadband can deliver speeds over 1 Gbps, making it fast enough to stream video and transfer large files.

data.targetWord: The physical or logical layout of how devices are connected together in a network — common examples include star, bus, and ring topologies

examples.en-GB: Choosing the right network topology affects the cost, reliability, and performance of a network.

data.targetWord: A key benefit of networking whereby devices connected to a network can share hardware (such as printers), files, and internet access

examples.en-GB: Resource sharing means a school only needs one printer per floor because all computers on the network can use it.

data.targetWord: The underlying physical equipment and connections that a network runs on — including cables, routers, switches, and servers

examples.en-GB: A WAN relies on telecommunications infrastructure such as fibre optic cables and satellites owned by ISPs.

data.targetWord: A folder or resource on a server that is made available to authorised users across a network

examples.en-GB: Pupils save their work to a network share so it is available from any computer in the school and backed up centrally.

data.targetWord: A device that creates a wireless local area network, typically connected to a wired network and transmitting a Wi-Fi signal for nearby wireless devices

examples.en-GB: Each floor of the school building has its own access point so that wireless devices can connect throughout the building.

data.targetWord: A router (or other device) that acts as the entry and exit point connecting a local network to external networks such as the internet

examples.en-GB: All internet traffic from the school LAN passes through the gateway router before reaching the wider internet.

data.title: Data Travelling from Computer to Website
data.instruction: Put these steps in the correct order to describe the journey of data from a computer on a LAN to a website on the internet.
items: User's computer sends data via its NIC
Data travels along the cable to the switch
Switch forwards the data to the router
Router sends the data out across the internet
Data arrives at the web server

data.title: Setting Up a Star Topology Network
data.instruction: Arrange these steps in the correct order to set up a star topology network for a small office.
items: Install a switch in a central location
Run an Ethernet cable from each computer to the switch
Connect the switch to the router
Connect the router to the ISP broadband connection
Configure DHCP on the router to assign IP addresses
Test each computer can access the network and internet
